Calling Psyche: NASA's Deep Space Network

Three Ears on Earth: NASA talks to faraway spacecraft through the Deep Space Network: giant antennas in California, Spain, and Australia. The three sites sit a third of the way around the world from each other. As Earth spins, one of them always faces Psyche.

Giant Dishes: Each site has one huge dish 70 meters (230 feet) across, plus several smaller dishes 34 meters (111 feet) across. Psyche talks through the 34-meter dishes. The site near Madrid, Spain, has six antennas, the most of any site.
Inside a Big Dish: Workers upgrade the 70-meter dish near Canberra, Australia in 2020. The white bowl is the dish itself.

Whispers from Space: Psyche's mainantenna is 2 meters (6.5 feet) across. It sends with 100 watts. By the time the signal reaches Earth, it can be as weak as a billionth of a billionth of a watt. The dishes send commands back with up to 20,000 watts.
Goldstone, California: The 70-meter dish at Goldstone, in the Mojave Desert. It was damaged in 2025 and is being repaired. The other 13 antennas keep every mission connected.

Waiting for Light: Radio travels at the speed of light, but space is huge. Light takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth. Psyche can be more than 4 times farther from us than that, so a hello and its reply take much longer. Near the asteroid, it can take over an hour round-trip, depending on where Earth and Psyche are. Try the PING button at Mission Control.
How Long to Say Hello?: A 34-meter dish at Goldstone, California. A message to Psyche can take over an hour round-trip, depeniding on where Earth and Psyche are.

Steering with Echoes: The network does more than carry messages. It helps steer. When Psyche moves away, its radio tone drops a little, like a passing siren. That gives its speed. Timing a signal there and back gives its distance. At the asteroid, tiny shifts in the signal will show how its gravity pulls on the spacecraft, and whether it hides a metal core.

The First Trip to a Metal World: NASA's Psyche spacecraft is flying to an asteroid that is also named Psyche. Scientists think it is rich in metal. Psyche launced on October 13, 2024, on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. It reaches the asteroid in 2029 and will orbit it for at least 26 months

The Asteroid: Psyche circles the Sun in the main asteroid belt, between Mars and Jupiter, about three times as far from the Sun as Earth is. It is about 173 miles (280 kilometers) across at its widest. Astronomers found it in 1852 , but no spacecraft has ever seen it up close. Its surface may be a mix of metal and rock.
What Might it Look Like?: An Illustration of asteroid Psyche. No one knows what it really looks like yet: the spacecraft will be the first to see.

Why Psyche? Planets like Earth have metal cores, far too deep and hot to ever reach. Psyche may be the exposed core of an early building block of a planet. Visiting it is a way to look inside a planet. It is also a new kind of world to explore: one made of metal, not just rock or ice.
The Route: Psyche loops around the Sun, swings past Mars in May 2026 for a speed boost, and arrives at the asteroid in August 2029.

How Psyche Flies: Psyche flies with Hall-effect thrusters that push out glowing blue xenon gas. Their push is gentle: about the weight of an AA battery resting on your hand. But they can fire for months, so Pyche keeps speeding up. The whole trip is about 2.2 billion miles.
Four Orbits: At the asteroid, Psyche will fly four orbits, A to D. The lowest, orbit D, is just 47 miles above the surface.

The Team Behind Psyche: Principal Investigator Lindy Elkins-Tanton leads the mission's science. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California manages the mission. Maxar Technologies (now Intuitive Machines) built the main body of the spacecraft. Psyche is the 15th mission in NASA's Discovery Program. Students help too: this book comes from the Psyche Student Collaborations Program.

A Flyby for Speed: On May 15, 2026, Psyche swung past Mars, just 2,864 miles above the surface. Mars' gravity bent Psyche's path and sped it up by about 1,000 miles per hour without using any fuel. The team also tested every instrument on Mars: a practice run for the asteroid
First Look: May 3, 2026: Psyche's camera spots Mars from about 3 million miles away. The colors were added to the picture.
The Crescent Grows: As Psyche closed in from May 2 to May 15, Mars grew bigger in every picture.
Brighter Than Expected: Dust in Mars' air scattered sunlight, so the crescent glowed brighter and reached farther around than the team expected.
Craters Up Close: Four pictures taken in six minutes, stitched together. This region includes Fournier crater, about 70 miles wide. Enhanced color shows different kinds of ground.
Ice at the South Pole: Just after its closest pass, Psyche photographed the ice cap at Mars' south pole.
Huygens Crater: Huygens crater in enhanced color, which makes small differences in the groound easy to see.
Next Stop: Psyche: Leaving Mars behind. Psyche reaches its asteroid in August 2029.
